title: Pauri 18: countless fools
hookLine: asankh moorakh: countless fools, thieves and liars too, and Nanak calls himself lowly (Japji 18)

lines: A LIST OF EVERYONE WHO'S WRONG.
cards: You know the feeling of reading the news and thinking: people are idiots. The driver who cut you off. The scammer.
The politician caught lying. Somebody's comment under a video. It's easy, and weirdly satisfying, to make a list of everyone who's wrong.
Pauri 18 makes that list. It's long, and it's harsh. And at the very end, the one making the list does something almost nobody does after a list like that.

teach.b: Pauri 17 counted the countless devoted. Pauri 18 counts the countless who've gone wrong, and it opens: asankh moorakh andh ghor. Countless fools, blind in deep darkness.
Then, in paraphrase: countless thieves, and people who live off what isn't theirs. Countless who rule by force and then are gone. Countless who cut throats and kill.
Countless who do wrong and keep doing it. Countless liars, wandering in their lies. Countless slanderers, carrying the weight of it on their heads.
It doesn't soften anything. Creation includes all of this, and it's countless too.
Then the last line, in the original: naanak neech kahai veechaar. Nanak, the lowly, offers this reflection. Neech means low, lowly.

Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh path, closes a list of fools and thieves by calling himself low. Commentators read it a few ways. Some hear pure humility: the one who speaks is no higher than anyone he's described.
Some hear something sharper: the speaker won't pretend he's outside the list.
Either way, it takes the sting of superiority out of the whole stanza. Then the refrain: I can't even once be a sacrifice to You. Whatever pleases You is good.
You are forever safe, Formless One. So the countless include the saints and the scoundrels, and the voice that names them stands low, among them, not above.

how: Pauri 18 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs point to its closing line, in which Guru Nanak calls himself lowly, as a model of humility.

o: a fool lost in deep darkness
high, exalted, seated on a throne

games.q: what's inside Pauri 18 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 18 only counts the good people of creation
it counts fools, thieves, tyrants, killers, liars and slanderers too.
at the end of Pauri 18, Guru Nanak calls himself lowly
naanak neech kahai veechaar: Nanak, the lowly, offers this reflection.
Pauri 18 ends with a different refrain from Pauri 17
it's the same: whatever pleases You is good; You are forever safe, Formless One.

games.q: you've just listed countless fools, thieves and liars. how does Guru Nanak end the stanza?
o: by thanking God he's not like them.
by calling for them to be punished.
games.why: naanak neech kahai veechaar: the one naming them stands low, among them, not above.

practice: Hold one opinion you feel strongly about other people, who's foolish, who's wrong, and ask: what if I'm missing something here? You don't have to drop it; just let it sit a little lower, a little less sure.
If a need to be right comes up, notice it, and let it soften as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Neech. Low, lowly: what Nanak calls himself, at the end of a pauri counting countless fools, thieves, tyrants and liars.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 18, last line: Nanak, the lowly, offers this reflection.

carryVoice: Your line: nanak the lowly. Humility, even at the end of a list of thieves and liars. That's day one hundred ninety.
